**Logical Clocks and Quorum Systems (written directly, not delegated):**

*Logical clocks.* (1) **Lamport timestamps** assign each event a scalar counter incremented on local events and updated to `max(local, received) + 1` on message receipt, producing a partial order consistent with **happens-before** (→): if a→b then L(a)<L(b), though the converse doesn't hold, so Lamport clocks can't detect concurrency. (2) **Vector clocks** fix this by having each process maintain a vector of counters, one per process; comparing vectors component-wise lets a system detect true concurrency versus causal precedence, which is exactly what Amazon **Dynamo** uses to detect conflicting sibling writes that the application (or a CRDT merge function) must reconcile. The related but distinct **version vectors** track per-replica write counts for data items rather than per-process event counts, used for replica divergence detection in systems like Riak. (3) **Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)**, used in CockroachDB and MongoDB, combine a physical wall-clock component with a logical counter so that timestamps stay close to real time (useful for human-readable snapshots and TTLs) while preserving the causality-tracking guarantee of Lamport clocks even when physical clocks skew. (4) Spanner's **TrueTime API** takes a different approach entirely: instead of logical counters, it exposes bounded clock uncertainty intervals `[earliest, latest]` from GPS/atomic-clock-synchronized timeservers, and achieves external consistency via **commit-wait**, delaying transaction commit until the commit timestamp is guaranteed to have passed in real time across all replicas.

*Quorum systems.* (1) The classic **Dynamo-style quorum** rule requires `R + W > N`, where `N` is the replication factor, `W` the number of replicas acknowledging a write, and `R` the number read; this guarantees at least one overlapping replica between any read and the latest write, giving quorum consistency without full synchronous replication. Dynamo additionally uses **sloppy quorums with hinted handoff**: writes during replica unavailability go to the next healthy nodes in the preference list and are later handed off to the proper owner, trading strict quorum intersection for availability. (2) **Paxos** relies on a different quorum property: any two majority quorums of acceptors must intersect, which is what guarantees safety (no two different values can be chosen) even though liveness requires only that some quorum eventually succeeds; **Raft** uses majority quorums analogously for both leader election and log commitment, requiring a log entry to be replicated to a majority before it's considered committed. (3) **Flexible Paxos** relaxes the classical requirement, showing phase-1 (leader election) quorums and phase-2 (replication) quorums need not be majorities of the same set, only that every phase-1 quorum intersects every phase-2 quorum, which allows smaller or asymmetric quorums for better fault-tolerance/latency tradeoffs. (4) **Witness replicas** (non-voting or storage-only members) and **weighted/grid quorum systems** generalize plain majority voting by assigning unequal votes or two-dimensional grid arrangements to replicas, letting operators tune fault tolerance versus latency without paying full replication cost everywhere.

# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging

**ARIES protocol.** The canonical WAL discipline, formalized in IBM's ARIES, enforces the **"log before data"** rule (write-ahead logging proper): a page's dirty in-memory state may only be flushed to disk after its corresponding log record is durably written. Every log record carries a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**, and every data page stores the LSN of the last log record that modified it (**pageLSN**), which recovery uses to determine whether a logged update is already reflected on disk. Commit durability is enforced via **force-log-at-commit**: the commit log record must be flushed to stable storage before the transaction is acknowledged as committed, though the data pages themselves can remain dirty in the buffer pool (**no-force, steal** buffer management).

**Log record types.** ARIES distinguishes **redo-only**, **undo-redo**, and **compensation log records (CLRs)**. A CLR is written when undoing an update during rollback; it is redo-only (never itself undone again), and it records a **next-undo-LSN** pointing to the next record to undo for that transaction, which is what makes rollback-of-rollback impossible and bounds undo work even if a crash occurs mid-rollback.

**Checkpointing.** ARIES uses **fuzzy checkpoints**: a `begin_checkpoint` record is written, then the current **dirty page table (DPT)** and **transaction table (active transaction list)** are captured and written out (possibly over time without blocking transactions), followed by an `end_checkpoint` record. Because the checkpoint doesn't force all dirty pages to disk, it's cheap, but it requires recovery to use the recorded DPT to know how far back in the log to scan.

**Group commit.** Because force-log-at-commit would otherwise serialize every commit behind an fsync, systems batch multiple transactions' commit records into a single log buffer flush (**group commit**), amortizing the fsync cost across many commits issued close together in time.

**Logging granularity.** ARIES uses **physiological logging**: log records are physical with respect to a single page (identified by page ID) but logical in how they describe the operation within that page (e.g., "insert this record at this slot"), which is cheaper than full physical before/after page images and more robust than purely logical logging across multiple pages.

**LSM-engine WAL.** In LSM-based engines like RocksDB, every write first goes to a WAL file and then to the in-memory **memtable**; the WAL exists purely for crash recovery of unflushed memtable contents and can be safely truncated once the memtable is flushed to an immutable SSTable, decoupling WAL retention from the engine's primary read/write path.

## 2. MVCC

**Snapshot-based tuple versioning.** PostgreSQL's MVCC stores multiple physical row versions with `xmin`/`xmax` system columns recording the creating and (if deleted/updated) invalidating transaction IDs. A transaction's **snapshot** (a set of "in-progress" XIDs and a cutoff) determines tuple visibility: a version is visible if its creator committed before the snapshot was taken and its deleter either hasn't committed or doesn't exist.

**Garbage collection of version chains.** Old row versions become **dead tuples** once no active snapshot can see them; PostgreSQL's **VACUUM** process reclaims this space, and InnoDB's **purge threads** remove undo-log entries once no active **read view** references them. Both mechanisms require tracking the oldest active transaction to know what's safe to reclaim.

**Write skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation prevents many anomalies but not **write skew**, where two transactions each read overlapping data, make disjoint writes based on stale reads, and together violate an invariant neither individually violated. PostgreSQL implements **SSI** (Cahill et al.'s algorithm) using **predicate locking** (SIREAD locks) to detect dangerous read-write dependency cycles between concurrent transactions and abort one transaction to preserve true serializability.

**Timestamp-ordering optimistic MVCC.** SQL Server's **Hekaton** (In-Memory OLTP) assigns each row version a **begin-timestamp/end-timestamp** pair and uses purely optimistic concurrency control: transactions execute against a snapshot without locking, then enter a **validation phase** at commit that checks for conflicting concurrent writes before installing the new versions, aborting on conflict rather than blocking.

**XID wraparound and freezing.** Because transaction IDs are fixed-width, PostgreSQL must periodically **freeze** old tuples (marking them visible to all transactions regardless of XID comparison) to avoid XID wraparound causing old committed data to spuriously appear in the future as "not yet committed."

## 3. LSM Trees

**Memtable/SSTable structure.** Writes land in an in-memory sorted structure (the **memtable**, often a skip list), which upon reaching a size threshold is flushed as an immutable **Sorted String Table (SSTable)** on disk. Immutability means SSTables need no in-place updates, only sequential append plus eventual compaction, which is the core LSM write-path advantage over B-trees.

**Compaction strategies.** **Leveled compaction** (LevelDB/RocksDB) organizes SSTables into levels with exponentially increasing size bounds (e.g., 10x per level), merging overlapping key ranges from level N into level N+1; this bounds space amplification tightly but increases write amplification since data is rewritten at each level. **Size-tiered compaction** (Cassandra-style) instead merges similarly-sized SSTables together regardless of key range overlap, reducing write amplification at the cost of higher space amplification and slower point reads (more files may need checking).

**Bloom filters.** Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** over its keys so point lookups can skip SSTables guaranteed not to contain the key, with a tunable false-positive rate trading memory for fewer unnecessary disk reads; false negatives are impossible by construction.

**Amplification tradeoffs.** LSM design is a three-way tradeoff among **write amplification** (bytes written to disk per logical byte written, inflated by repeated compaction rewrites), **read amplification** (number of SSTables/levels checked per read), and **space amplification** (ratio of on-disk size to logical data size, inflated by not-yet-compacted obsolete versions and tombstones).

**Tombstones.** Deletes are recorded as **tombstone** markers rather than immediate removal; the actual space is reclaimed only when compaction merges the tombstone with the data it shadows, which is why deletes in LSM systems temporarily increase space usage rather than decreasing it.

**Block indexing.** Within an SSTable, a sparse **block index** maps the first key of each data block to its file offset, so a lookup does a binary search on this small in-memory index and then a single block read/scan rather than scanning the whole SSTable.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splitting.** On leaf overflow, a new leaf is allocated, keys are redistributed (typically 50/50), and the split key is propagated up as a new separator in the parent; if the parent also overflows, the split propagates recursively, and a split at the root increases tree height by one, which is the only way a B+tree grows taller.

**Node merging/redistribution.** On deletion causing underflow (a node falling below its minimum fill threshold), the tree either **redistributes** keys from a sibling (if the sibling has surplus) or **merges** the underflowed node with a sibling, removing a separator key from the parent, potentially cascading underflow upward.

**Lehman-Yao / B-link trees.** Classic latch-coupling (crabbing) down the tree during concurrent access is prone to deadlock and poor concurrency during splits. The **Lehman-Yao algorithm** adds a **right-link pointer** from each node to its right sibling (the **B-link tree** structure); a reader that lands on a node mid-split can simply follow the right-link to find keys that moved during the split, allowing lock-free (or single-node-latch-only) concurrent traversal without holding multiple latches simultaneously.

**Fill factor and bulk loading.** Index builds specify a target **fill factor** below 100% to leave room for future inserts without immediate splitting; bulk loading from sorted input can construct a B+tree bottom-up in one pass, which is far cheaper than repeated single-row insertion.

**Prefix/key compression.** Leaf pages commonly apply **prefix compression**, storing only the differing suffix of consecutive keys that share a common prefix, increasing the effective fan-out per page and reducing tree height.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit

**Prepare and commit phases.** A coordinator sends a **PREPARE** message to all participants; each participant durably logs its intent and replies **VOTE-COMMIT** or **VOTE-ABORT**. If all vote commit, the coordinator writes a **global commit decision** record and sends **COMMIT** to all participants; if any votes abort, it sends **GLOBAL-ABORT**. Each participant acknowledges, and the coordinator can then discard transaction state.

**The blocking problem.** If the coordinator crashes after sending PREPARE but before the final decision reaches a participant, that participant is left **in-doubt**: having voted commit, it must hold all locks (it cannot unilaterally abort, since others may have committed) until the coordinator recovers and resends the decision, which can block resources indefinitely. This is 2PC's defining weakness relative to non-blocking consensus protocols.

**Presumed abort/commit optimizations.** **Presumed abort** lets participants assume a transaction aborted if they have no record of it after a coordinator failure (avoiding the need to log abort decisions at all, since "no record" implies abort), reducing log writes for the common case of aborts. **Presumed commit** inverts this assumption for workloads where commits dominate.

**WAL of the decision.** The coordinator's commit/abort decision record must itself be flushed to its own log (force-write) before participants are told to commit, so that coordinator recovery after a crash can correctly replay the already-made decision rather than re-deciding and potentially contradicting what some participants already did.

**Three-phase commit.** **3PC** inserts a **pre-commit** phase between prepare and commit, so that participants can determine the right action independently of coordinator failure as long as no more than a bounded number of nodes fail and the network isn't partitioned, making it non-blocking under those assumptions, at the cost of an extra round trip; it does not tolerate network partitions, which limits its practical adoption.

**Standards and relation to consensus.** The **XA standard** defines the vendor-neutral prepare/commit interface used by application servers and heterogeneous resource managers (databases, message queues) to coordinate 2PC across different products. **Paxos Commit** (used conceptually in systems like Spanner) replaces the single coordinator with a Paxos group acting as coordinator, eliminating the single point of blocking failure while keeping the two-phase vote structure.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport timestamps.** Each process keeps a scalar counter, incremented on every local event and set to `max(local, received)+1` on message receipt. This produces a total order consistent with **happens-before**: `a → b` implies `L(a) < L(b)`, but the converse doesn't hold, so Lamport clocks alone cannot distinguish true causal precedence from mere coincidence of timestamp ordering, i.e., they can't detect concurrency.

**Vector clocks.** Each process maintains a vector of counters, one slot per process, incrementing its own slot on local events and taking the elementwise max on message receipt (plus incrementing its own slot). Component-wise comparison of two vectors tells whether one happened-before the other or whether they're concurrent, which is exactly the information Dynamo-style systems use to detect conflicting sibling writes needing application-level or CRDT-based reconciliation. **Version vectors** are the related but distinct per-replica (not per-process) analogue used to track how far each replica has propagated a given data item's updates.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** Used in CockroachDB and MongoDB, HLC timestamps combine a physical wall-clock component with a logical tie-breaking counter, so timestamps stay close to real wall-clock time (useful for human-readable snapshots, TTL expiry, and bounding clock-skew-related staleness) while still guaranteeing the Lamport causality property even when physical clocks are skewed or jump.

**TrueTime and commit-wait.** Google Spanner departs from logical counters entirely: its **TrueTime API** exposes a bounded uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` for "now," synchronized via GPS and atomic clocks. Spanner achieves external consistency through **commit-wait**: a transaction delays returning commit success until its assigned commit timestamp is provably in the past everywhere, guaranteeing that a later transaction observing the effect gets a strictly greater timestamp in real time.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Dynamo-style quorums.** The rule **R + W > N** (reads plus writes needed exceeds total replicas) guarantees any read quorum and any write quorum share at least one common replica, ensuring a read can observe the latest acknowledged write without requiring all N replicas to participate in every operation.

**Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff.** Rather than failing writes when the "natural" owning replicas are unavailable, Dynamo routes writes to the next healthy nodes on the preference list (a **sloppy quorum**) and later replays them to the correct owners once they recover (**hinted handoff**), trading strict quorum-overlap guarantees for availability during partial failures.

**Paxos quorum intersection.** Paxos's safety proof rests on the fact that any two majority quorums of acceptors must intersect in at least one acceptor; this shared acceptor is what prevents two different values from both being chosen. Raft uses the same majority-quorum principle for both **leader election** (a candidate needs votes from a majority) and **log commitment** (an entry is committed once replicated to a majority of followers).

**Flexible Paxos.** This result shows the phase-1 (leader election) quorum and phase-2 (replication) quorum don't both need to be majorities of the same set; safety only requires that every phase-1 quorum intersects every phase-2 quorum, which opens the door to asymmetric quorum sizing for better latency/fault-tolerance tradeoffs than plain majority Paxos.

**Witness replicas and weighted quorums.** **Witness replicas** vote in quorum decisions without storing full data (reducing storage cost while still contributing to fault tolerance), and **weighted/grid quorum systems** assign unequal votes or arrange replicas in two-dimensional grids to let operators tune the tradeoff between read/write quorum size and fault tolerance independently of raw replica count.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** Recovery proceeds in three phases: **Analysis** scans the log forward from the last checkpoint to reconstruct the transaction table and dirty page table as they existed at crash time; **Redo** replays all logged updates from the minimum recorded pageLSN forward (even for transactions that will later be undone, which is the "repeat history" principle), bringing the database to the exact state at crash time; **Undo** then rolls back all transactions that were active (uncommitted) at crash time, in reverse log order.

**Idempotent redo via LSN comparison.** Redo is made idempotent by comparing each log record's LSN against the target page's current **pageLSN**: if the page's pageLSN is already ≥ the record's LSN, the update is skipped as already applied, which allows redo to be safely re-run even if a previous recovery attempt was itself interrupted by another crash.

**CLR-driven undo.** During the Undo phase, each rolled-back update generates a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**, which is redo-only and will never itself be undone; this is what makes recovery from a crash-during-rollback safe, since re-running recovery again will redo the CLRs already written rather than re-undoing the same operation.

**Checkpoint bounding.** The fuzzy checkpoint's recorded dirty page table gives the Analysis phase a firm starting point and a minimum pageLSN to redo from, bounding how far back in the log a crash recovery must scan; without checkpoints, recovery would need to scan the entire log history since the database's creation.

**Media recovery vs. crash recovery vs. rollback.** These are distinct mechanisms: **transaction rollback** undoes one transaction's effects during normal operation (e.g., on explicit ROLLBACK or deadlock abort); **crash recovery** restores the database to a consistent state after an abrupt process/OS failure using the WAL as described above; **media recovery** restores from a full backup plus replayed WAL/archive logs after physical storage loss (disk failure, corruption), a fundamentally different scenario requiring a base backup rather than just in-place log replay.

**Torn-write protection.** Because a crash can occur mid-write of a multi-sector page, leaving a **torn page** (partially old, partially new data), InnoDB uses a **doublewrite buffer**, writing pages to a contiguous staging area before writing them to their final location, so a torn final write can be detected and repaired from the doublewrite copy; PostgreSQL instead relies on **full-page writes** in the WAL (the first modification to a page after a checkpoint logs the entire page image) plus page checksums to detect corruption.

---

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas (write-ahead logging, MVCC, LSM trees, B+tree maintenance, two-phase commit, logical clocks, quorum systems, and crash recovery), each with at least three specific named mechanisms treated in technical depth using standard terminology (e.g., ARIES/LSN/CLR/fuzzy checkpoints for WAL and crash recovery; xmin/xmax snapshots, SSI predicate locking, and Hekaton timestamp-ordering for MVCC; leveled vs. size-tiered compaction, Bloom filters, and amplification tradeoffs for LSM trees; Lehman-Yao B-link trees and split/merge propagation for B+tree maintenance; prepare/commit phases, presumed abort, and 3PC for two-phase commit; Lamport/vector clocks, HLC, and TrueTime for logical clocks; R+W>N, sloppy quorums, and Paxos/Raft majority intersection for quorum systems).

response.content:
## Write-Ahead Logging

**ARIES-style WAL protocol.** Every update to a page generates a log record before the page itself is written to stable storage — the "log before data" rule (WAL invariant): the log record describing a change must reach durable storage before the dirty page it describes can be flushed. Each log record and each page carries a log sequence number (LSN), a monotonically increasing identifier (typically a byte offset into the log). Every page header stores a `pageLSN`, the LSN of the most recent log record that modified that page. Transaction commit requires force-log-at-commit: the commit log record (and everything preceding it) must be flushed to stable storage before the commit is acknowledged to the client, guaranteeing durability (the D in ACID) without requiring data pages to be flushed synchronously. This decouples buffer pool flushing (which can be lazy, driven by the background writer/checkpointer) from transaction durability.

**Log record types.** ARIES distinguishes several record kinds. *Redo-only* records describe a physical/physiological change sufficient to reapply it but carry no undo information (used for operations like page allocation that are not transactionally undoable in the normal sense). *Undo-redo* records are the common case for ordinary updates — they carry both the after-image (or diff) needed for redo and enough before-image/inverse-operation information for undo. *Compensation log records* (CLRs) are written during transaction rollback (either explicit abort or undo-phase recovery) to record that an undo action has been performed; a CLR is redo-only (it is never itself undone) and contains a `UndoNxtLSN` field pointing to the next record to undo in that transaction's backward chain, which lets rollback skip over already-undone work and makes rollback itself logged and idempotent — rolling back a rollback never happens.

**Checkpointing.** ARIES uses fuzzy checkpoints rather than consistency-point (quiesce-all) checkpoints. A checkpoint writes a `begin_checkpoint` record, then asynchronously gathers the dirty page table (DPT, mapping each dirty buffer-pool page to its `recLSN`, the LSN at which it first became dirty) and the transaction table (TT, listing active transactions and their `lastLSN`), and writes an `end_checkpoint` record containing these structures (or pointers to them, since they can be large and are written incrementally). Transactions and page flushes continue concurrently during this process — hence "fuzzy." A master record (or equivalent) stores the LSN of the most recent `begin_checkpoint`, giving recovery its starting point. PostgreSQL's checkpointer is analogous: it flushes dirty shared-buffer pages and records a REDO pointer (the WAL LSN from which recovery must begin) rather than requiring a global quiesce.

**Group commit and log buffering.** Log records are appended to an in-memory log buffer and flushed via `fsync`/`fdatasync` in batches rather than one syscall per commit. Group commit lets multiple transactions committing in a narrow time window share a single flush: the first committer to request a flush "sweeps up" the commit records of transactions that queued behind it, amortizing the fixed cost of a disk flush/fsync across many commits. InnoDB exposes this via `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit` (0/1/2, trading durability for throughput) and a configurable log buffer; PostgreSQL has `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings` and relies on `wal_writer` plus group commit in `XLogFlush`.

**Logging granularity.** *Physical logging* records exact byte-level before/after images of pages. *Logical logging* records higher-level operations (e.g., "delete key K from index"), which is compact but complicates recovery because a logical operation's effect on physical page structure may depend on concurrent structure changes (e.g., B-tree splits). ARIES uses **physiological logging**: records are physical in that they apply to one specific page by page ID, but logical in that the change within the page can be described at the operation level (e.g., "insert this record at this slot") rather than exact byte diffs. This is InnoDB's approach for most row/index changes and ARIES's documented compromise.

**WAL in LSM engines.** RocksDB writes every mutation to a write-ahead log file before inserting it into the active memtable; the WAL entry uses a monotonic sequence number analogous to an LSN. On flush, once a memtable is persisted as an SSTable, the corresponding WAL segment becomes obsolete and can be recycled/deleted — flush durability is tracked by comparing the memtable's max sequence number against flushed SSTable metadata. RocksDB supports `WAL_ttl` and synchronous (`sync=true`) vs. asynchronous writes, and can disable WAL per-write for bulk loads at the cost of durability on crash.

## Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** *Analysis* scans forward from the last checkpoint's `begin_checkpoint`/REDO-pointer, reconstructing the transaction table and dirty page table as they stood at crash time, determining the set of loser transactions (active, uncommitted) and the `RedoLSN` — the minimum `recLSN` across the DPT, which is the earliest point redo must start. *Redo* scans forward from `RedoLSN`, reapplying every logged update whose target page's on-disk `pageLSN` is less than the log record's LSN (repeating history for both committed and uncommitted transactions, since undo needs the physical page state consistent). *Undo* scans backward from the transaction table, rolling back all loser transactions by following each one's `lastLSN`/`prevLSN` chain, writing a CLR for each undone action.

**Idempotent redo.** Comparing a log record's LSN against the page's current `pageLSN` makes redo idempotent: if `pageLSN >= record LSN`, the update is already reflected on the page (perhaps the page was flushed before the crash) and the record is skipped. This allows recovery to be re-run safely if it itself crashes mid-recovery.

**CLRs and repeating history.** Because undo during recovery (or normal abort) writes CLRs that are redo-only and chained via `UndoNxtLSN`, a second crash during recovery simply re-triggers Analysis/Redo/Undo; redo reapplies already-written CLRs idempotently and undo resumes from wherever the transaction table indicates, guaranteeing recovery terminates correctly regardless of how many times it is interrupted.

**Checkpoints bound recovery.** The `RedoLSN`/DPT from the most recent fuzzy checkpoint bounds how far back the log scan must go — without checkpoints, Analysis/Redo would need to scan to the start of the log. PostgreSQL similarly uses the checkpoint's REDO pointer to bound WAL replay.

**Scope distinctions.** *Transaction rollback* undoes one transaction's effects via normal abort processing while the system is up. *Crash recovery* restores the whole database to a transaction-consistent state after an unplanned shutdown, using the log alone. *Media recovery* restores from a base backup plus archived/replayed WAL after physical loss of a storage device, a strictly disjoint, typically much longer, log-replay operation (PostgreSQL PITR, Oracle RMAN).

**Torn-write protection.** Because pages are often larger than the atomic write unit of the underlying storage, a crash mid-write can produce a torn page, part old part new data. InnoDB's doublewrite buffer writes pages to a contiguous staging area before writing them to their final location, so a torn page can be detected and repaired from the doublewrite copy during recovery; many engines additionally store a page checksum so corruption/tearing is detectable independent of repair mechanism. PostgreSQL mitigates torn pages via `full_page_writes`, logging the entire page image the first time it's modified after a checkpoint.

response.content:
# MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

## Snapshot isolation and tuple visibility

PostgreSQL implements MVCC by storing multiple physical versions of a row (tuple) and tagging each with `xmin` (the XID of the transaction that created the version) and `xmax` (the XID of the transaction that deleted or superseded it, or 0/invalid if live). A transaction acquires a *snapshot* at (depending on isolation level) statement start or transaction start, consisting of a list of XIDs active at that moment plus the next-to-assign XID. Tuple visibility is determined by comparing a candidate tuple's `xmin`/`xmax` against the snapshot: a tuple is visible if its creating transaction committed before the snapshot was taken (not in the snapshot's active list, and XID < snapshot's xmax cutoff) and either `xmax` is invalid or belongs to a transaction that aborted or is itself invisible to the snapshot. Commit status is resolved via the commit log (`pg_xact`/CLOG), caching hint bits on the tuple header to avoid repeated CLOG lookups. This gives **Snapshot Isolation (SI)**: readers never block writers and vice versa, since readers simply ignore versions not yet committed-visible.

InnoDB achieves the same semantics differently: it keeps the current row in place and maintains a *rollback segment* (undo log) of prior versions, reconstructing old versions on demand by walking the undo chain, driven by a `DB_TRX_ID` tuple field and a **read view** (InnoDB's analogue of a snapshot) listing active transaction IDs at snapshot-open time.

## Version chains and garbage collection

Old versions must eventually be reclaimed. PostgreSQL's **VACUUM** process scans tables for dead tuples — those whose `xmax` committed and are no longer visible to any active snapshot (determined via the global "xmin horizon," the oldest xmin among active snapshots) — and marks their space reusable, additionally removing corresponding index entries. Without timely vacuuming, dead tuple accumulation causes table/index bloat. InnoDB instead uses background **purge threads** that process the undo log asynchronously once no read view can still need old-version undo records, trimming the rollback segment's history list.

## Write skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

Snapshot Isolation avoids classic dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and (unlike plain Read Committed) phantom reads within a transaction's own snapshot, but it does **not** prevent **write skew**: two concurrently running transactions each read overlapping data, and each writes to disjoint tuples based on values the other has concurrently changed, producing a final state no serial execution could produce (the canonical example: two doctors each checking that at least one of them is on call before taking themselves off, both succeeding, leaving zero on call). SI also permits anomalies like read-only transaction skew. To close this gap, PostgreSQL implements **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, which layers predicate locking (SIREAD locks) on top of ordinary MVCC snapshots: it tracks rw-antidependencies (a read by T1 that a later write by T2 would have affected) without blocking readers, and aborts one transaction when it detects a "dangerous structure" — a cycle of rw-antidependencies among concurrent transactions — that could produce a serialization anomaly. This yields true serializable isolation (`SERIALIZABLE` in PostgreSQL) at a cost of occasional serialization-failure aborts requiring client retry.

## Optimistic MVCC with begin/end timestamps (Hekaton)

SQL Server's Hekaton (In-Memory OLTP) engine uses a lock-free, latch-free optimistic MVCC scheme oriented entirely around logical timestamps rather than XIDs. Each row version carries a `Begin-Ts`/`End-Ts` pair denoting the logical time range during which it is valid. Transactions read a consistent snapshot by comparing their own start timestamp against each version's Begin/End range, with no locking taken during the read or write phase. At commit, a **validation phase** checks (a) visibility rules still hold for all reads, (b) no write-write conflicts occurred against rows the transaction updated, and under serializable isolation (c) phantom avoidance via revalidating scan predicates — before the transaction's end timestamp is finalized and installed, making it durable only after validation succeeds; failed validation forces abort and retry, characteristic of **optimistic concurrency control (OCC)** rather than pessimistic locking.

## XID wraparound and freezing

PostgreSQL's XID is a 32-bit counter; since visibility comparisons use modulo-2^32 circular arithmetic, exhausting the XID space would cause old transactions to appear to be "from the future," corrupting visibility. **Freezing** rewrites a tuple's `xmin` to a special `FrozenXID` sentinel once it is guaranteed visible to all future transactions, removing dependence on the literal XID value; VACUUM performs this, and PostgreSQL forces aggressive "anti-wraparound" vacuums when the oldest unfrozen XID approaches the wraparound danger zone.

## Version-aware indexing

Multi-version B-trees (e.g., the MVBT structure) extend standard B-trees so each index entry carries a validity time range, enabling efficient point and range queries "as of" an arbitrary past timestamp without reconstructing from logs. InnoDB and PostgreSQL approximate this more crudely: index entries point to the primary/heap tuple, and visibility filtering happens post-index-lookup rather than being timestamp-encoded in the index structure itself, trading index simplicity for extra heap visibility checks.

---

# Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

## Mechanics: prepare and commit phases

2PC coordinates atomic commitment of a distributed transaction across multiple resource managers under a single **coordinator** (transaction manager) and multiple **participants** (resource managers). **Phase 1 (prepare/voting phase):** the coordinator sends `PREPARE` to all participants; each participant makes its updates durable (writes an undo/redo-capable prepare record to its own log), then replies `VOTE-COMMIT` if it can guarantee the ability to commit, or `VOTE-ABORT` otherwise, and if voting commit, it must hold all locks on affected resources until told the outcome. **Phase 2 (commit/abort phase):** the coordinator collects votes; if all are `VOTE-COMMIT` it writes a *global commit* decision record to its own log (this is the durability-forcing point) and sends `GLOBAL-COMMIT` to all participants; if any vote `VOTE-ABORT` (or times out), it decides abort and sends `GLOBAL-ABORT`. Participants apply the decision, release locks, and acknowledge.

## The blocking problem

2PC is fundamentally a **blocking protocol**: if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted commit but before the global decision is delivered, those participants are left **in-doubt** — holding all locks and unable to unilaterally decide commit or abort, since another participant may have voted abort (if the coordinator decided abort) or committed. They must block until the coordinator recovers and consults its log, or until a human/heuristic intervention occurs, during which contended resources remain locked, stalling unrelated transactions. This is the central liveness weakness of 2PC and motivated non-blocking alternatives.

## Presumed abort / presumed commit

Standard 2PC requires the coordinator to log and retain outcome records indefinitely to answer in-doubt participant queries after recovery, and requires acknowledgments to be logged. Two optimizations reduce log volume:
- **Presumed abort**: if the coordinator has no record of a transaction, it assumes abort was the outcome (since abort records can be omitted — not logging a decision at all defaults to abort on recovery query). This eliminates abort-record writes and ACK logging for aborts, important because aborts are often the frequent/early-exit case.
- **Presumed commit**: inverts the default so the absence of a log record implies commit, beneficial when most transactions commit; it eliminates the need to log and retain commit records and participant acknowledgments, at the cost of needing a more careful protocol for garbage-collecting prepare records.

Both are specified as part of the XA/X-Open distributed transaction model and widely implemented in commercial TP systems and database XA drivers (e.g., Oracle, DB2, and via `XA START/PREPARE/COMMIT` in MySQL/InnoDB's XA support).

## Write-ahead logging of the 2PC decision

Correctness of 2PC's durability guarantee rests on classic **write-ahead logging (WAL)** discipline applied to the coordinator: the global commit (or abort) decision record must be flushed (forced) to stable storage *before* the coordinator sends the outcome to participants or before participants release locks and report success upward, ensuring that even if every process crashes immediately afterward, the decision can be deterministically recovered and replayed rather than re-derived by polling potentially-crashed participants.

## Three-phase commit (3PC)

**3PC** inserts an additional *pre-commit* phase between voting and committing to make the protocol non-blocking under the assumption of a synchronous network (bounded message delay) and no network partitions: after collecting unanimous `VOTE-COMMIT`, the coordinator sends `PRE-COMMIT` (not yet the final commit) and waits for acknowledgments before issuing the final `COMMIT`. This extra round lets participants that time out during phase 2 safely infer the outcome (e.g., if a participant received pre-commit, it knows all participants voted commit and can unilaterally proceed) by electing a new coordinator from surviving participants rather than blocking indefinitely. 3PC's limitation is that it only guarantees non-blocking termination under synchrony and the absence of network partitions; under asynchronous networks or partitions it can still violate safety (inconsistent decisions across partitioned subgroups) or liveness, which is why it saw little production adoption relative to its theoretical appeal.

## Relation to distributed consensus and XA

2PC is not itself a consensus protocol because the coordinator is a single point of failure/blocking; **Paxos Commit** (Gray and Lamport) generalizes 2PC by replacing the single coordinator with a Paxos-replicated group that runs consensus on each participant's vote, so coordinator failure no longer blocks progress as long as a quorum of the replicated coordinator group survives — effectively running 2PC's voting phase "underneath" a fault-tolerant consensus layer. Google **Spanner** uses this idea directly: each Spanner transaction's participant group leaders run Paxos for replication, and cross-shard transactions use 2PC among participant leaders (one acting as the overall coordinator), with TrueTime-based timestamps providing external consistency; the coordinator's own commit record is itself replicated via Paxos, eliminating the classical single-coordinator blocking failure mode. The **XA** standard (X/Open Distributed Transaction Processing) formalizes the participant-facing interface (`xa_prepare`, `xa_commit`, `xa_rollback`, `xa_recover`) that lets a transaction manager coordinate heterogeneous resource managers (multiple RDBMSs, message queues) via exactly this prepare/commit protocol, and is the interoperability layer most commercial and open-source databases (Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB, message brokers like ActiveMQ) implement to participate in externally coordinated 2PC.

response.content:
# LSM Trees

**Memtable and SSTable structure.** Writes land first in an in-memory **memtable**, typically a skip list (LevelDB, RocksDB default) or a red-black tree, ordered by key. The write is also appended to a write-ahead log (WAL) for durability before being acknowledged. When the memtable reaches a size threshold, it is frozen (made immutable) and flushed to disk as an **SSTable** (Sorted String Table): an immutable file of key-value pairs sorted by key, organized into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 4-16 KB in RocksDB), each block optionally compressed. Each SSTable carries a **sparse index** — typically one index entry per block, mapping the block's first/last key to its file offset — rather than a dense per-key index, trading a small amount of extra scanning within a block for a much smaller index held in memory. A footer holds metadata pointers to the index block, a **Bloom filter** block, and block-compression statistics. Because SSTables are immutable once flushed, all mutation is handled by writing new SSTables and later reconciling duplicate/overwritten keys via **compaction**; this immutability simplifies concurrency (readers never need locks on SSTable contents) and enables simple crash recovery (replay WAL, rebuild memtable).

**Compaction strategies.** Two dominant families exist. **Leveled compaction** (LevelDB, RocksDB's default `kCompactionStyleLevel`) organizes SSTables into levels L0, L1, ..., Ln, each with a target size typically 10x the previous (the "level size multiplier" or fanout, configurable, commonly 10 in RocksDB). L0 files come straight from memtable flushes and may have overlapping key ranges; L1+ are maintained as non-overlapping sorted runs. Compaction picks a file (or a few) from Li, merges it with overlapping files in Li+1, and writes the merged, deduplicated result back into Li+1. This bounds read amplification (at most one file per level needs checking for a point lookup, barring L0 overlap) and space amplification (roughly 1.1x the data size per level) at the cost of higher **write amplification**, since each key may be rewritten once per level it passes through (commonly cited as 10-30x total write amplification for a 10x fanout with many levels). **Size-tiered compaction** (Cassandra's default, also an option in RocksDB via `kCompactionStyleUniversal`) instead groups SSTables of similar size into "tiers"; when enough similarly-sized tables accumulate (e.g., 4), they are merged into one larger table of the next tier. This reduces write amplification (each byte is rewritten O(log(N)) times total rather than once per level) but increases space amplification, since multiple generations of overlapping, un-merged tables can coexist, and increases read amplification, since a point read may need to probe one file per tier.

**Bloom filters.** Each SSTable (or each block) stores a Bloom filter over its keys — a probabilistic bit-array membership structure with k hash functions — allowing point lookups to skip SSTables that provably do not contain the key, at the cost of a tunable false-positive rate (RocksDB defaults to ~1% with 10 bits/key). False positives cause an unnecessary disk read/seek but never a false negative, so correctness is preserved; the tradeoff is purely a space/CPU-vs-I/O knob, since more bits per key shrinks the false-positive rate but grows the filter's memory/disk footprint. This directly attacks **read amplification**, the number of physical I/Os needed to answer a logical read, which in LSM trees is inherently worse than in a B+tree because a key may be live in the memtable or in any level's SSTable.

**Tombstones and amplification tradeoffs.** Deletes are written as **tombstone** markers (a key with a special delete marker and sometimes a TTL) rather than removing data in place, since SSTables are immutable. Tombstones are only physically reclaimed when compaction merges the SSTable containing the tombstone with all SSTables containing the shadowed older versions of that key — deferred, compaction-time garbage collection. Until that happens, tombstones consume space (space amplification) and must be scanned over on reads. Cassandra's "tombstone problem" — pathological read latency when many tombstones accumulate without being compacted (e.g., from range deletes) — is a direct, well-known consequence. Overall, LSM design is a three-way tradeoff space: leveled compaction minimizes space/read amplification at higher write amplification; size-tiered minimizes write amplification at higher space/read amplification.

# B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splitting and merging.** On insertion into a full leaf, the leaf **splits**: keys are divided (typically at the median) into two leaves, and a copy of the separator key is inserted into the parent internal node, pointing to the new right sibling. If the parent is also full, this **split propagates upward** — the internal node splits similarly, promoting a separator key one level further up — and if the root splits, a new root is created, increasing tree height by one. Deletion can cause **underflow** (a node falling below its minimum occupancy, commonly 50% of capacity). Classic B-tree algorithms respond with **redistribution** (borrowing a key from an adjacent sibling through the parent, rebalancing without changing tree shape) or, when siblings are also at minimum occupancy, **merging/coalescing** two nodes into one and removing the now-redundant separator from the parent, which can itself underflow and propagate the merge upward, potentially shrinking tree height. Many production systems (InnoDB, PostgreSQL's nbtree) skip immediate merging on delete for performance, instead allowing pages to become sparse and relying on background vacuum/purge processes or lazy merge-on-next-split logic, since strict eager merging/splitting on every delete causes excessive I/O ("thrashing" near the underflow threshold).

**Concurrency control via B-link trees and Lehman-Yao.** Naive concurrent B+tree access requires **latch coupling** (a.k.a. crabbing): a thread holds the latch on a parent node only until it has acquired the latch on the relevant child, then releases the parent's latch, ensuring safe downward traversal without holding the whole path locked. This is pessimistic and serializes splits badly. The **Lehman-Yao algorithm** improves on this with the **B-link tree**: every node gets a **right-link (sibling) pointer** to its right neighbor at the same level, plus a "high key" marking the upper bound of keys it's responsible for. When a node splits, the new right sibling is linked in via the right-link *before* the parent's pointer is updated, so a concurrent reader who latches a node mid-split and finds the target key larger than the node's high key simply follows the right-link rather than failing or waiting. This allows searches to proceed with only a single latch held at a time (no coupling needed) and makes splits a localized, nearly lock-free operation; the structure is sometimes called "half-latched" since only writers performing a structural modification need to latch multiple nodes briefly. ARIES/KVL (key-value locking), used in IBM-style and derivative systems, layers higher-level, longer-duration key-range locks for transaction isolation on top of this short-duration physical latching, separating logical concurrency control from physical page concurrency control.

**Bulk loading, fill factor, and compression.** Bulk loading a B+tree (e.g., building a secondary index from an existing table) bypasses repeated single-key insertion and splitting by sorting all keys first and building leaf pages bottom-up at a target **fill factor** below 100% (InnoDB and PostgreSQL commonly target ~90% leaf fill) to leave room for subsequent inserts without immediate splits, trading some space for lower future write amplification. Within leaf pages, **prefix compression** (storing only the differing suffix of a key relative to the previous key in the page, as in InnoDB's compact row format) and more general key/value compression reduce page footprint, increasing the effective fanout per I/O and improving cache hit rates, at the cost of CPU to decode during scans and more complex in-page insertion logic.
